argument.name: The Thomistic Proof (from the real distinction between essence and existence)
argument.overview:
Feser's formal statement has 36 steps, which fall into six phases.

1. **Steps 1–11: the real distinction.** Three independent lines of argument show that, in the things we experience, essence and existence are really (not just conceptually) distinct: (a) we can know a thing's essence without knowing whether it exists (2–3); (b) the things of experience are contingent, not necessary (4–5); (c) there could be at most one thing whose essence is its existence, yet the things of experience come, or could come, in many (6–10).
2. **Steps 12–18: dependence here and now.** A thing with really distinct essence and existence cannot give itself existence, so it must receive it from a distinct cause — and since the distinction persists at every moment, it must receive it at every moment, including now.
3. **Steps 19–23: the first cause.** The cause is either another such thing or something whose essence is existence. A series of the former is hierarchical, so it cannot regress infinitely; its first member must be subsistent existence itself.
4. **Steps 24–27: uniqueness and universality.** There can be only one subsistent existence itself, so everything else has distinct essence and existence and therefore depends on it: it is the cause of everything other than itself.
5. **Steps 28–33: attributes.** It is necessary, uncaused, and purely actual, and so (by chapter 1's reasoning) immutable, eternal, immaterial, incorporeal, perfect, omnipotent, fully good, intelligent, and omniscient.
6. **Steps 34–36: conclusion.** Such a cause is what we mean by God; so God exists.

Notice two features. First, the whole argument turns on one pivot: **whatever merely *has* existence must receive it; only what *is* existence need not.** Second, the argument is about what sustains things **now**, not about a beginning in time.

stages.title: Stage 1a — The real distinction between essence and existence
stages.gist: Three arguments (knowability, contingency, uniqueness) show that in every thing we experience, what it is and that it is are really distinct aspects of reality.

stages.title: Stage 1b — Existence must be imparted here and now
stages.gist: Nothing can give itself existence, so each such thing depends on a distinct cause for its existence at every moment it exists.

stages.title: Stage 1c — The regress terminates in subsistent existence itself
stages.gist: The series of existence-imparting causes is hierarchical, so it needs a first member, which can only be something whose essence just is existence.

stages.title: Stage 2a — Unique cause of everything else
stages.gist: Since there can be only one thing whose essence is existence, everything else depends on it for existence.

stages.title: Stage 2b — The divine attributes
stages.gist: Subsistent existence itself is necessary, uncaused, and purely actual, and so has all the attributes that follow from pure actuality.

stages.title: Conclusion — God exists
stages.gist: A unique, necessary, uncaused, purely actual cause of all that sustains everything in being is God.

steps.text: For each of the things we know from experience — stones, trees, dogs, people, and so on — we can distinguish its essence (what it is) from its existence (that it is).
steps.why: This much is simply the observation Feser opens with: knowing that a human is a rational animal is different from knowing that humans are really out there. The open question is only whether the distinction is real or merely verbal, like ‘bachelor’ vs. ‘unmarried man’.

steps.text: If the distinction were not real — a distinction in things themselves rather than just in how we think or speak — then knowing what a thing is would by itself tell us whether it exists.
steps.why: A thing's essence is part of its objective reality, and so is its existence if it has one. If these were the very same feature of reality, grasping the one would be grasping the other.

steps.text: But knowing a thing's essence does not by itself tell us whether it exists.
steps.why: The lion/pterodactyl/unicorn test: a full description of their natures does not reveal which one exists, which is extinct, and which never existed. And denying a lion's existence is a false judgment, not a misconception of what a lion is — unlike denying that a lion is a cat.

steps.text: If the distinction were not real, the things we know from experience would exist necessarily rather than contingently.
steps.why: If existence belonged to a thing simply by virtue of what it is, it would exist by its very nature and could not fail to exist.

steps.text: But in fact these things exist only contingently, not necessarily.
steps.why: They come into being and pass away; lions might never have existed and may one day go extinct. Their need for causes and their vulnerability to destruction presuppose that existence is not part of what they are.

steps.text: If there could be more than one thing whose essence is identical to its existence, they would have to be distinguished from one another either as species within a genus, or as members of a single species, or in some other way.
steps.why: Two things are two only if something differentiates them. The two standard ways are by a specific difference (as rationality marks off humans among animals) or by matter (as Socrates and Plato are distinct parcels of the same humanity); step 6 leaves room for any other way too.

steps.text: But such things could not be distinguished in any of these ways.
steps.why: Any differentiating factor — a specific difference, a parcel of matter, or anything else — would make each one ‘existence itself PLUS something’, so neither would really be that which is simply existence itself.

steps.text: So there could not, even in principle, be more than one thing whose essence is identical to its existence.
steps.why: Follows from 6 and 7: every possible way of making two such things fails.

steps.text: So, for any of the things we know from experience, if its essence and existence were not really distinct, there could not be more than one of its kind.
steps.why: Follows from 8. If essence and existence are not really distinct, they are identical (there is no middle option of existence being a mere ‘part’ of the essence), and anything like that would be one of a kind.

steps.text: But for each of the things we know from experience, there is, or at least could be, more than one of its kind.
steps.why: There are many stones, trees, dogs, and people; and even where a kind is down to its last member, there could be more.

steps.text: So, for each of the things we know from experience, the distinction between its essence and its existence is a real distinction.
steps.why: Follows from 9 and 10 (modus tollens), and is independently supported by 2–3 and by 4–5. Three separate routes converge on the same conclusion.

steps.text: Anything whose essence is really distinct from its existence must have existence imparted to it either by itself or by some cause distinct from it.
steps.why: Its existence does not follow from its essence (as a circle's properties follow from its essence), so it must be conferred; and the only options are self or other.

steps.text: If it imparted existence to itself, it would be the cause of itself.
steps.why: Imparting existence to oneself just is causing one's own existence.

steps.text: Nothing can be the cause of itself.
steps.why: To act — including to impart existence — a thing must already exist. A thing that must receive existence would therefore have to exist before it exists in order to cause itself to exist, which is incoherent.

steps.text: So it cannot impart existence to itself.
steps.why: Follows from 13 and 14.

steps.text: So anything whose essence is really distinct from its existence must have its existence imparted by some cause distinct from it.
steps.why: Follows from 12 and 15: of the two options, the first is ruled out.

steps.text: Because such a thing's essence and existence remain really distinct at every moment it exists, including right now, its existence must be imparted by a distinct cause at every moment it exists, including right now.
steps.why: The Fido point: the real distinction does not disappear once Fido has been conceived. At every instant his existence still doesn't follow from his essence and still can't be self-supplied, so at every instant something else must be supplying it — or he would blink out of existence.

steps.text: So each of the things we know from experience has its existence imparted to it by a distinct cause at every moment it exists, including here and now.
steps.why: Apply 16 and 17 to the things of experience, which by 11 all have really distinct essence and existence.

steps.text: This cause is either something whose own essence is distinct from its existence, or something whose essence and existence are identical — something that just is subsistent existence itself.
steps.why: These two options are exhaustive; the ‘middle ground’ of existence being merely part of an essence was shown to collapse into the second option.

steps.text: If the cause is something whose essence is distinct from its existence, then it too needs a distinct cause imparting existence to it at every moment it exists, including now.
steps.why: Steps 16–17 apply to anything whose essence is distinct from its existence, not just to the things we observe. So Fido's cause C needs B, and B needs A, all right now.

steps.text: The series of causes this generates is hierarchical, and a hierarchical series cannot regress infinitely but must have a first member.
steps.why: Each member imparts existence only insofar as it is simultaneously receiving existence from the one above it — its causal power is entirely derivative (instrumental). As chapter 1 argued, derivative causes without an underived source explain nothing, however many of them there are (the IOU point).

steps.text: This first member can only be something whose essence and existence are identical — something that just is subsistent existence itself.
steps.why: The first member must impart existence without having to receive it. Anything whose essence is distinct from its existence must receive it (16), so the first member cannot be like that; by 19 it must be subsistent existence itself.

steps.text: So each of the things we know from experience has its existence imparted to it at every moment, including now, either directly or through intermediaries, by a cause whose essence and existence are identical — subsistent existence itself.
steps.why: Follows from 18 through 22.

steps.text: Since there cannot be more than one thing whose essence is identical to its existence, this cause which is subsistent existence itself is unique.
steps.why: Follows from 8.

steps.text: Since it is unique, everything else that exists must be something whose essence is distinct from its existence.
steps.why: Follows from 24 together with the exhaustiveness of the two categories (19): if only one thing can be of the second kind, everything else is of the first.

steps.text: Anything whose essence is distinct from its existence has its existence imparted to it, directly or indirectly, by the cause which is subsistent existence itself.
steps.why: The reasoning of 16–23 applies to any such thing whatsoever — including immaterial things such as angels or souls, if they exist — not only to the things of experience.

steps.text: So this unique cause which is subsistent existence itself is the cause of everything other than itself.
steps.why: Follows from 25 and 26. Note that the claim about ‘everything’ (and so the whole universe) is a conclusion here, not a premise — which is why the fallacy-of-composition charge misses.

steps.text: Since anything without a real distinction between its essence and existence would exist necessarily rather than contingently, this unique cause exists necessarily.
steps.why: Draws on the principle behind step 4: what exists by its very essence cannot fail to exist. Subsistent existence itself is the limiting case — its essence is existence.

steps.text: Whatever is subsistent existence itself neither needs, nor could have had, a cause of its own.
steps.why: A cause would have to impart existence to it; but it has nothing that receives existence — it is existence. This is why ‘What caused God?’ misfires: God is not an exception to a rule, but lacks the very feature (distinct essence and existence) that generates the need for a cause.

steps.text: So this unique cause which is subsistent existence itself is uncaused.
steps.why: Follows from 29.

steps.text: If subsistent existence itself had some potentiality for existence needing to be actualized, existence would have to be imparted to it by some cause.
steps.why: Essence stands to existence as potency to act: an essence distinct from its existence is a mere potential thing until existence actualizes it. Having such a potency would make it just another receiver of existence.

steps.text: So subsistent existence itself has no potential for existence needing actualization; it exists in a purely actual way.
steps.why: Follows from 30 and 31: since it is uncaused, it cannot have a potency that a cause would have to actualize. This is the bridge to chapter 1's purely actual actualizer — and since there can be only one purely actual thing, they are the same being.

steps.text: Whatever is purely actual must be immutable, eternal, immaterial, incorporeal, perfect, omnipotent, fully good, intelligent, and omniscient.
steps.why: Established in chapter 1 (and developed in chapter 6): change, temporal succession, and matter all involve potentiality; perfection and goodness are a matter of actuality; the source of all actualization has all power; and by the principle of proportionate causality the cause of all things must contain their forms in the way an intellect does, and so knows all things.

steps.text: So each of the things we experience has its existence imparted to it at every moment by a cause which is subsistent existence itself: one, necessary, the uncaused cause of everything else, purely actual, immutable, eternal, immaterial, incorporeal, perfect, omnipotent, fully good, intelligent, and omniscient.
For such a cause to exist is for God to exist.
steps.why: This is what classical theism means by ‘God’: not one more being among beings but the one who is existence itself, sustaining all things, with the attributes just listed. (Chapter 6 develops the divine attributes and why they belong to one and the same God.)

steps.text: So God exists.
steps.why: Follows from 34 and 35.
